brief.logline: For ten minutes every school morning, a parent's kids wait behind a strip of painter's tape across the kitchen doorway, clutching their emergencies, until the last drip falls through the hand-glazed Solace dripper.
brief.premise: A school morning. Across the kitchen doorway runs a strip of blue painter's tape, laid over older strips gone grey and scuffed where toes have stood. The kettle clicks. A parent sets the hand-glazed Solace dripper on a chipped mug and starts pouring by hand. The seven-year-old arrives first, one shoe on, the other held out with its lace in a knot, toes exactly on the tape. The thirteen-year-old comes next with a permission slip, a pen, and the parent's phone buzzing in her other hand. The small toes creep over the line; without looking up from the phone, she hooks them back behind it with her foot. Nobody speaks: the pour, the drip, one long sigh from the doorway, the phone buzzing until it gives up. The parent doesn't turn around; they know exactly who is there. The last drip falls. The parent lifts the dripper off the mug, sets it on the counter, turns, and takes the first sip facing the tape. Then they step over it, cup in hand, into everybody talking at once, and the used dripper sits on the counter in the only quiet spot left in the house.

what_makes_it_specific: Kept: 'The ten minutes of making coffee by hand are the only part of a parent's morning nobody interrupts.' The coffee is made by hand, and nobody interrupts it.
Obvious version: a frazzled parent gets away from the kitchen chaos for a slow, quiet pour-over and a peaceful first sip while the house roars off-screen.
Differs by what it costs someone: the interruptions are not off-screen. They stand at a tape line holding a knotted shoe, a permission slip and a buzzing phone, and they choose to wait.

Product role: any dripper would give the spot its clock, so the drip alone would make the product decoration. Instead the film ends on the one thing in the kitchen that was made the same slow way the coffee was: the used dripper under 'Solace. Glazed by hand.', the only words on screen. This breaks 'restraint over explanation' on purpose, because the picture can't show hand-glazing. The line is a verified fact, not a claim, and it is not a voiceover. Swap in a mass-made plastic or glass dripper and the last frame has nothing to say. 'One cup at a time' stays off the card until A01 is answered.

Detail Lucas didn't write: the painter's tape across the doorway, a fresh blue strip on top of older strips gone grey and scuffed where toes have stood, so the rule reads as years old without a word (A07; taste: one real detail per scene; restraint over explanation).

Rule shown, not told: the teenager hooks the small toes back behind the tape without looking up from the phone. The kids keep the rule themselves, which stops the tape reading as a parent shutting them out (A07).

Build: live action assumed (A09). 1 location. 3 fictional on-camera roles (parent, child about 7, teen about 13; A03) and 3 consistent characters. No voiceover or scripted lines; the closing chatter is background only. 0 lip-synced lines. 0 generated shots. About 5 shots of hands with the product (filter, pour, lift, set down, first sip; the filter shot depends on A02). 1 end-frame line. No product reference supplied (A02).

Make-or-break (A07): the doorway, not the drip. With no words, tape on a floor has to read as a rule the kids keep, not a half-finished paint job and not a parent shutting children out. First test: a silent 10 s mock-up in a real doorway with layered real tape, two stand-ins and the hook-back. Strangers who haven't read the brief answer 'why are they standing there?'. It passes if they say something like 'they're waiting for the parent to finish'. Any answer about paint or punishment switches to A07's fallback.

Second test (A06, a risk but not the make-or-break): a silent phone mock-up with a stand-in ceramic dripper on an opaque mug. Viewers who haven't read the brief say 'now' when they think the brew has ended. If they miss the last drip, the lift carries the cue alone, and the premise already has that beat.
Cost flag (children, in the waiting beats): cheaper version shoots them as feet on the tape and hands holding objects, with faces only in the closing chatter. The hook-back is feet only.
Cost flag (hands pouring hot water, in the pour beat): cheaper version uses one continuous pour take and builds the cutaways from the kids waiting, not from more product setups.
Alternative (not briefed): as the parent steps over the tape, the teenager's other parent steps behind it holding their own mug. The house passes the ten minutes on, one cup at a time.

evidence.specificity: "The thirteen-year-old comes next with a permission slip, a pen, and the parent's phone buzzing in her other hand. The small toes creep over the line; without looking up from the phone, she hooks them back behind it with her foot." The page names objects, actions and sounds at development level, which is enough for the creative director to build routes. The build count is exact: "1 location. 3 fictional on-camera roles ... 0 lip-synced lines. 0 generated shots. About 5 shots of hands with the product". It stays at 8 rather than 9 because the strategist would still need to ask what "Signal: link taps and product-page sessions from those paid social placements (A04, A05)" assumes. Neither ID is defined anywhere on the page.
evidence.distinctiveness: "a strip of blue painter's tape, laid over older strips gone grey and scuffed where toes have stood". The same goes for D03's "the parent steps over and takes the pen for the permission slip, not the phone" and the logline's "clutching their emergencies". None of these would survive a move to another brief. The obvious version is a pitch a rival would really make ("a frazzled parent gets away from the kitchen chaos ... while the house roars off-screen"). The work differs by who pays for it, not by tone. It stays at 8 because the page admits "any dripper would give the spot its clock". Another maker's hand-glazed ceramic dripper would pass the swap test everywhere except the end card.
evidence.fit: "Kept: 'The ten minutes of making coffee by hand are the only part of a parent's morning nobody interrupts.'" The premise takes Lucas's line literally and makes it sharper: the interruptions stand at the door and choose to wait. Verified facts are handled with discipline: "'One cup at a time' stays off the card until A01 is answered." The end card uses only verified words, and the break from a taste note is declared: "This breaks 'restraint over explanation' on purpose". It stays at 8 because the objective covers only the 9:16 cutdowns. The craft brief also requires every assumption in plain sight, and this page doesn't meet that.
evidence.craft: "Any answer about paint or punishment switches to A07's fallback." There is no A07 on the page. The brief cites A01–A09, A11 and A12, and A10 never appears. It has no assumptions table (ID | type | load-bearing | claim | if_wrong). So if the make-or-break test fails, it leads to a fallback that isn't written. The objective's signal (A04) and all five questions to Lucas also cite IDs he can't look up. A senior producer would catch this on first read. Everything else could be signed today. The logline is 33 words. The premise is 194 words and ends on its last sentence, and story_seed.ending repeats that sentence exactly. Video totals 60+20+15+6 = 101 s. The 9:16 labels put an event in motion by 1 s and the product by 3 s. Each cost flag sits next to a cheaper version, and the runner-up format is named with its reason. Smaller slips: D01's beat is two sentences, and the D02/D03 payoff handoffs aren't in the hero, yet the labels say they reuse hero footage.

normalized_brief.logline: For ten minutes every school morning, a parent's kids wait behind a strip of painter's tape across the kitchen doorway, clutching their emergencies, until the last drip falls through the hand-glazed Solace dripper.
normalized_brief.premise: A school morning. Across the kitchen doorway runs a strip of blue painter's tape, laid over older strips gone grey and scuffed where toes have stood. The kettle clicks. A parent sets the hand-glazed Solace dripper on a chipped mug and starts pouring by hand. The seven-year-old arrives first, one shoe on, the other held out with its lace in a knot, toes exactly on the tape. The thirteen-year-old comes next with a permission slip, a pen, and the parent's phone buzzing in her other hand. The small toes creep over the line; without looking up from the phone, she hooks them back behind it with her foot. Nobody speaks: the pour, the drip, one long sigh from the doorway, the phone buzzing until it gives up. The parent doesn't turn around; they know exactly who is there. The last drip falls. The parent lifts the dripper off the mug, sets it on the counter, turns, and takes the first sip facing the tape. Then they step over it, cup in hand, into everybody talking at once, and the used dripper sits on the counter in the only quiet spot left in the house.

content.audience_tension: Who: parents who make the day's first coffee at the kitchen counter while the school run gathers behind them. A shoe needs tying, a slip needs signing and their own phone is buzzing, all before the cup is poured. This behavior and moment come from the brief's [audience] field and the premise. They are the client's wish and the film's content, not research. Media proxy: parents of school-age children on Meta Reels/Stories. The two buying cells are defined in assumptions; they are buying assumptions, not research, and H11 decides between them. Tension [H1]: In their voice: I give the kids every other minute of the morning and I don't begrudge them one, yet I want the first coffee to be mine, and I'd hate to admit I'd make them wait for it. What they'd hate to admit: for a few minutes they would put a cup of coffee ahead of their children, and that feels selfish. Asking why once more shows this is about how they see themselves, not about time. Remove the product and the tension still holds, because it is about wanting one thing that is theirs, not about coffee gear. How the proposition settles it. What the film shows (premise content, not proof that it works): the kids wait behind the tape. The teenager, 'without looking up from the phone, she hooks them back behind it with her foot' (premise). Then 'The last drip falls. The parent lifts the dripper off the mug, sets it on the counter, turns, and takes the first sip facing the tape' (premise), and 'they step over it, cup in hand, into everybody talking at once' (story_seed.ending). The end frame is 'the used dripper, grounds still in it, under 'Solace. Glazed by hand.'' (must_include). What we hope viewers conclude: the kids keep the rule themselves [H2], the wait has an end the doorway can see [H5], and the parent goes to them as soon as it ends, so the wait cost nobody [H1(b), H2]. The parent has to believe that conclusion to stop feeling selfish. The film shows it and never says it (taste: restraint over explanation). The end frame then names the dripper by the fact that sets it apart, F3 [H12]. Rejected drafts: H7 (the unused ritual) and H8 (the gift-giver). The price objection is kept as the barrier hypothesis H9, because asking why once more collapses it into H1.

content.product_relevance: Moment: a school morning at the kitchen counter. The kettle has just clicked. The parent is pouring by hand through the dripper on a chipped mug while a shoe, a slip and a phone collect at the doorway. What goes wrong without it (H5, a category belief, not a fact): a coffee that makes itself doesn't need the parent's hands and has no end anyone can see. The house has no reason to wait and nothing to wait for, so the parent is fair game from the kettle click. A wait with no visible end also starts to look like shutting the kids out. What fixes it: F1 'Solace makes a ceramic pour-over dripper.' F1 proves the product is a pour-over. That a pour-over is poured by hand and ends on a last drip the doorway can see is category knowledge held in H5, not a verified fact. The pour occupies the parent. The last drip and the lift give the wait its visible end. That end is the film's sound-off cue (A06) and the reason the wait can cost nobody. F3 'The dripper is glazed by hand.' The dripper that makes the hand-poured coffee was glazed by hand. That is all the end frame says. A dripper glazed by machine cannot say it; a rival also glazed by hand could (H4). Blocked: needs a verified fact that the dripper is formed by hand, not only glazed. Until then, nothing may say or imply that the whole dripper is handmade: not this page, not the routes, not development's product-role note ('made the same slow way the coffee was'). Blocked: needs a verified fact that the dripper sits directly on a mug and brews into it (A01, A02) before the chipped-mug pour can be shown as how it is used. Without that fact, the pour could show a use the product doesn't have. Until A01 is answered, no line may imply single-cup brewing. Barrier (H9): a $38 (F2) dripper reads as kit for coffee hobbyists, or as money spent on themselves, not as something for a parent's school morning. With no product photos yet (A02), viewers also can't see what they would buy. Permission: not established. F3 is Solace's own claim. A viewer could check it only if the product page shows the glaze varying from unit to unit, which needs the A02 photos. Holds with no logo and no price: yes. The tape, the pour and the last drip carry it, and the end frame states only F3. Scene that must land: the last drip, the lift, the first sip facing the tape, then the step over. Feeling it should leave: the wait cost nobody anything, and the parent went to them. Taste: dry over sentimental, and restraint over explanation. The guilt stays in the picture, and nobody on screen names it or explains the tape. The end-frame line is development's deliberate break of 'restraint over explanation', because the picture can't show glazing. Strategy keeps the break: of the facts on this page, F3 is the one that narrows the field (H4).

hypotheses: H1 Riskiest (two halves, scored separately): parents of school-age kids (a) want the first coffee to be theirs, and (b) would hate to admit they'd make the kids wait for it. The pull is guilt about wanting something for themselves, not a shortage of time. The proposition's 'a wait that costs nobody' rests on (b). Test (a), walkthrough: six interviews with parents who make coffee during the school run. Each walks through their last school morning, and nobody mentions rituals, guilt, coffee gear or waiting. Recruit quota: at least three of the six make coffee with a machine, pod or instant today, so the same six also test H5, and the screener tests H6. Kills (a) if: fewer than three of six raise, unprompted, wanting something in the morning that is theirs. Test (b), projective: a walkthrough would rarely surface (b), because it is what they'd hate to admit, and that test would kill a true belief. So test it later in the same session, after the walkthrough so it can't prime it. Show the same six parents H2's silent doorway mock-up, no release and no product name, and ask only 'What do you make of this parent?' If H2's frame doesn't already include the parent, add a stand-in's back at the counter in the same take. Otherwise it adds no cost. Kills (b) if: fewer than three of six, unprompted, judge the parent for making the kids wait, whether they defend it, envy it or call it selfish. Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist (Lucas to recruit). If (a) survives and (b) dies, the proposition drops 'a wait that costs nobody' and falls back to the want alone: 'A dripper glazed by hand, for the pour nobody interrupts.' (10 words, nearer Lucas's key_message). H2 then has to guard harder against the wait reading as shutting the kids out. If (a) dies, the tension fails and the strategy goes back to Lucas.

H2: the fresh tape over older grey strips, together with the hook-back, reads as a rule the kids keep. It must not read as an unfinished paint job or a parent shutting children out (A07). This is also what makes 'a wait that costs nobody' visible. Test: development's silent 10 s mock-up in a real doorway with layered real tape, two stand-ins and the hook-back, shown to unbriefed strangers who are asked 'why are they standing there?'. Owner: Director. Kills it if: any viewer answers paint or punishment; switch to A07's fallback. Answers from the six H1(b) parents about paint or punishment count here too.

H3: the buyer is the parent who drinks the coffee, not a partner or relative buying a gift (A08). Test: Solace's order data (share of orders with gift notes, or with a shipping name that differs from the billing name), or a one-question post-purchase poll. Owner: Lucas / Solace. Kills it if: gifts are the majority of orders; re-aim the tension at the giver (H8).

H4 (rival swap, rerun on the new proposition, plus an unrun market check). Swap result: put a rival's name in front of 'a dripper glazed by hand, for a wait that costs nobody' and it reads true only if that rival's dripper is also glazed by hand. It reads false for drippers glazed by machine, for glass, plastic or metal drippers, and for machines and pods (if H5 holds). The previous line, 'Your first coffee, poured by hand, is a wait that costs nobody', read true for every pour-over. So the redraft narrows the field from every pour-over to hand-glazed drippers, but it is not Solace-only. Belief: no rival hand-glazed dripper brand currently leads its advertising with a parent's morning or a wait at the counter, and hand-glazing is not already the category's standard opening line. Test: review current ads (Meta Ad Library, YouTube) and the product pages of ceramic and hand-glazed dripper brands before routes lock. Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist (needs a research tool; unrun, raised as a blocker). Kills it if: a hand-glazed rival already leads with a parent's protected morning, or most ceramic dripper brands lead with hand-glazing, which would make F3 table stakes. The proposition then needs a Solace-only fact. A01 may supply one if 'one cup at a time' means each dripper is glazed one at a time, and the formed-by-hand question may supply another.

H5 (category common knowledge, not a fact): a hand pour keeps the parent's hands busy and ends on a last drip the doorway can see, while a machine or pod brews unattended with no visible end. That is why the house waits for this and would not wait for a machine, and why the wait can cost nobody. Test: in the H1(a) walkthrough, the machine, pod and instant users (at least three, by quota) describe what happens while their coffee brews, without anyone mentioning interruptions. Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist. Kills it if: machine users describe the same protected window, which would make the product decoration.

H6: the audience mostly makes coffee with a machine, pod or instant today, so these are new pour-over buyers, not existing dripper owners. Test: the H1 recruit screener logs pour-over ownership for every parent screened, not only the six chosen, because the quota fixes the six. Add a one-question Stories poll on Solace's account. Owner: Brand and Audience Strategist. Kills it if: most screened parents already own a pour-over. The job then becomes replacement, which needs a verified reason to switch that we don't have.

H7 Rejected tension (the unused ritual). In their voice: I bought something nice so I could make coffee slowly, yet on school mornings I gulp it at the door, and the thing I bought for myself sits there unused. Rejected because it speaks to existing owners and casts pour-over as the thing that fails them. Revive if: H6 fails and most of the audience already owns a pour-over.

H8 Rejected tension (the giver). In their voice: I want to give my partner their mornings back, yet I can't give them time, only things. Rejected because the brief's audience is the parent at the counter. Revive if: H3 shows that gifts are most orders.

H9 (barrier): the price itself is not what stops the tap or the purchase. What stops it is that a $38 dripper reads as coffee-hobbyist kit, or as money spent on themselves. Test: an open-answer exit poll on the product page during the flight ('What stopped you today?'). Owner: Lucas / Solace. Kills it if: 'too expensive' leads the open answers. Then the product page, not the film, has to carry value.

content.recommendation_rationale:
Pick R1. The proposition, 'A dripper glazed by hand, for a wait that costs nobody', lands at 43-52 s. The hand waits until the drips stop and lifts the dripper, and the parent turns to sip facing the tape without having refused anyone. With the dripper the sharpest thing in every waiting frame, R1 best serves the pre-flight criterion (4 of 5 muted viewers call 'now' at the lift and name the dripper) and D02's lift-reach rate. D02 is the cut it serves, and its master frame gives S01 and D04 as labelled.
Gives up [changed]: F3 doing any work. R2 builds 'by hand' into the story: a small hand lays the rule, the parent's hands pour, and the line names the glaze. R1 trades that for the clearest muted release. R1 also fails the rival swap test until A02 and H4 are answered, because its drain says 'not yet' for any pour-over (H5), and its only Solace-only link, the glaze mark, depends on a sample nobody has. It gives up the open admission that the parent goes first (R3). The hook-back reads on an insert, not in the main frame.
Failure: D02 17-20 s (D01 56-60 s). At phone size the glaze mark can read as a chip in a film that has already shown a chipped mug. The fix comes in stages. (1) The mug has left in the parent's hand, so nothing chipped shares the end frame. (2) The window key rakes across the glaze so the mark reads as glaze, without framing it larger than the grounds. (3) Check it in the H12 viewing. (4) If it still reads as damage, drop it from the end frame; the thumb at the lift keeps it in the film, and the line carries F3 alone. If A02 shows that not every unit carries a mark, both go before the shoot.
Kill test [changed]: the muted D02 first cut gets 'now' at the lift, but viewers say the parent is ignoring the kids, not that the kids are waiting for the parent to finish. The drain is reading as the parent's no, so the idea fails, not the craft. Switch to R3. Its post-release line, with the parent serving each held thing in turn, cup in hand, is the only route that shows the wait cost nobody. R2 would not fix it: it answers who set the rule, not whether the parent pays the wait back.
Case R2 [changed]: H2 (must_include A07), punishment answers. If the silent doorway mock-up gets 'they're being made to stand there', A07's fallback still triggers, as the brief sets. R2 is the route to carry into that retest, because it is the only one that shows in picture who lays the tape. It does nothing for 'paint' answers and may add to them; those stay with A07's fallback alone. Also H3: if gifts are most orders (H8), 'given, not taken' re-aims at the giver with the least rework.
Case R3 [changed]: audience_tension H1(b). If the H1(b)/H2 viewing survives with three or more of six parents calling the doorway parent 'selfish' or 'shutting them out', the guilt is live and the release alone won't settle it. R3 admits the parent goes first and pays the line back, object by object. If H1(b) dies, R3 has no guilt left to answer either.

evidence.specificity: A writer, casting and design can build from these routes without calling back. Every beat names an object, an action and a sound. For example, R1: "22-28 s [P*, rec, first try: phone-to-floor insert; fb G+C: generated feet and phone hand over the floor plate]: The small toes creep over. A sneaker hooks them back, and the lit phone at the top of frame never lowers. Nobody reacts." Each colour is tied to an object: "Colours: #2E6FB7 fresh tape, #A39E93 old grey tape strips, #EFE8DA chipped mug, #7A5C3E floorboards." The open questions (glaze colour, glaze mark, a window in the base) are real A02 blockers and are flagged as such, not left vague. It stops at 8 for two reasons. D02 and D03 are only timed at 1 s and 3 s. And some blocking does the director's job and earns nothing here: "The parent is at frame right, the kids in the back plane."
evidence.distinctiveness: Two routes add something only this idea could have. R2: "From the hall side, a small hand presses a fresh blue strip flat over the grey ones and never goes past the line." R3: "Parents go last, except at the counter." The recommended route, though, fails the craft brief's rival-swap test, and it says so itself: "What it costs on F3: any pour-over's drain says 'not yet' (H5). In this idea 'hand-glazed' is the dripper's name, not its logic." Everything distinctive in R1 comes from Lucas's premise (the tape, the hook-back). R1's only Solace-only link is a glaze mark that "depends on a sample nobody has." R1's and R3's 9:16 cutdowns are also close to interchangeable (toe by 1 s, pour, cone drains, isolated lift, sip, step-over, end frame), so on the paid unit the idea stops being distinctive.
evidence.fit: Every must-include is present in all three routes. The must-avoids hold, and claims stay tightly within the verified facts: "Never shown: a lingering shot of steam (heat), a pleased face at the sip (taste), any count of cups (A01)." Lucas's premise is kept beat for beat, and anything added is flagged as a question for Lucas. But the pick drops half of the single-minded proposition ('A dripper glazed by hand, for a wait that costs nobody'), and the rationale admits it: "Gives up [changed]: F3 doing any work." The strategy's pre-flight criterion (1) tests whether the kids are read as waiting for the parent to finish, on a muted D02 mock-up. Yet neither R1's nor R3's D02 contains the hook-back (A07), the must-include that makes that reading possible.
evidence.craft: The structure is professional. D01 beats run back to back from 0 to 60 s. P* tags carry fallbacks, and the kill test is a real idea-level failure: "Kill test [changed]: the muted D02 first cut gets 'now' at the lift, but viewers say the parent is ignoring the kids, not that the kids are waiting for the parent to finish." Each Case names a brief field (H2, H3, H1(b)). Four problems keep it below 8. (1) The named failure rests on a mark that may never exist: "Failure: D02 17-20 s (D01 56-60 s). At phone size the glaze mark can read as a chip in a film that has already shown a chipped mug." (2) R3 squeezes the scene the strategy says must land into 5 s: "30-35 s [P* hand on product, then face; fb R+C for the lift, G+C profile for the sip]: The wide. The hand waits over the dripper until the sound stops, lifts it and sets it at the head of the line." (3) The rationale credits R1 with the clearest muted release, but all three D02s use the same "isolated lift insert (H10)". (4) "the water sinks to a flat bed of grounds" is a barista quality signal inside the product, which implies a brewing claim.
